Large language models (LLMs) and agent systems increasingly support scientific discovery across domains. Yet the literature remains fragmented around isolated tasks, with limited attention to how components form integrated workflows. Here, we introduce exploration, hypothesis generation, and testing (EXHYTE) as an empirical workflow abstraction for reviewing AI-assisted scientific discovery. We mapped a corpus of recent studies to EXHYTE stages and substages to identify recurring strategies, workflow connections, and capability gaps. The analysis shows strong progress in exploration, especially retrieval, knowledge assembly, and representation learning as well as growing capacity for hypothesis and idea generation. led prioritization, testing, and refinement across chemistry, materials, biomedicine, and general scientific reasoning.
Discussion and future outlook
This survey synthesizes recent work on AI for scientific discovery through the EXHYTE framework, an operational workflow lens for organizing how LLMs and agentic systems support (or approximate)
Explore
,
Hypothesize
, and
Test
functions. Using this lens, we unify a fast-growing and heterogeneous literature, surface stage-specific strengths and gaps, and highlight where current systems fail to compose into robust end-to-end discovery workflows. Because EXHYTE organizes systems by workflow function rather than by agent architecture, the same lens applies to role-partitioned multi-agent scaffolds and to the newer paradigms now entering the field, tool-use systems, standardized tool-access (MCP-style) protocols, coding agents with explicit plan-then-execute loops, and computer-use agents that drive software and instruments through their interfaces. Rather than requiring a new stage for each architecture, these map onto existing substages: tool use corresponds to retrieval and knowledge assembly (E2-E3) and tool-grounded experimental design (T1), plan-then-execute behavior to protocol generation and computational testing (T1–T2), and reflection or critique mechanisms to prioritization and refinement (H2, T2).
Stage-level maturity and bottlenecks
Our synthesis finds that Explore is the most mature stage, driven by rapid progress in literature retrieval, RAG pipelines, knowledge-graph construction, and representation learning. However, this maturity is uneven: most systems treat literature as the primary evidence source, while comparatively few analyze real scientific datasets to identify patterns, anomalies, confounders, or mechanistic gaps that would initiate genuinely data-driven discovery. In contrast, Hypothesize remains underdeveloped beyond generation: many systems can propose ideas, but fewer provide rigorous mechanisms for novelty checking, plausibility assessment, or principled prioritization under explicit constraints. The weakest link remains Hypothesize → Test: translating promising hypotheses into executable experimental plans with reliable evaluation signals and then using those signals to refine or reject hypotheses. The Test stage also lags in practice: most systems remain
in silico
, and the few that incorporate wet-lab validation typically depend on substantial human supervision and bespoke infrastructure. Two further gaps sit at the workflow’s edges rather than within any single stage: trigger formation, problem finding, and assessment of which questions are worth pursuing remain largely human-supplied, since systems enter through human-defined inputs rather than identifying their own problems; and even systems that connect multiple stages stop short of full automation, because evidence interpretation, hypothesis revision, and scientific value judgment still require human checkpoints.
Scope and limitations of EXHYTE as an operational lens
EXHYTE is not intended as a comprehensive theory of all scientific change. It best characterizes data-intensive, tool-mediated inquiry where progress proceeds through iterative exploration, hypothesis formulation, and empirical appraisal. Important dimensions of scientific practice are only partially represented in current systems mapped onto EXHYTE. First, paradigm shifts and other forms of “revolutionary” change involve broader conceptual re-framings and shifts in standards of evidence that are not well captured by present-day computational workflows. Second, scientific knowledge is stabilized through external validation and organized skepticism, including community scrutiny, replication, and credit/prioritization mechanisms, which extend beyond closed-loop internal scoring. Third, human scientific judgment extends well beyond ranking or approving machine-generated outputs: domain intuition, problem selection, interpretive judgment, and contextual understanding shape what counts as a meaningful research question and what constitutes adequate evidence. This last point also carries a risk that grows as workflows automate more substages: heavy reliance on AI for retrieval, idea generation, and appraisal may erode the very capacities—critical reading, independent judgment, and the ability to frame and recognize a worthwhile problem—that these systems presuppose in their human users. We therefore treat the preservation of human judgment not as a temporary scaffold to be removed as systems mature but as a standing requirement for trustworthy discovery. Throughout this survey, we accordingly treat EXHYTE as a pragmatic framework for mapping AI system capabilities and integration points, while explicitly noting where essential social and epistemic mechanisms remain outside the loop. Although the importance of MYCN amplification in this disease is indisputable, the mechanistic details remain enigmatic. Here, we present a multicellular model of neuroblastoma comprising a continuous automaton, discrete cell agents, and a centre-based mechanical model, as well as the simulation results we obtained with it. The continuous automaton represents the tumour microenvironment as a grid-like structure, where each voxel is associated with continuous variables such as the oxygen level therein. Each discrete cell agent is defined by several attributes, including its cell cycle position, mutations, gene expression pattern, and more with behaviours such as cell cycling and cell death being stochastically dependent on these attributes. By implementing a stochastic simulation algorithm on modern GPUs, we simulated the dynamics of over one million neuroblastoma cells over a period of months. Specifically, we set up 1200 heterogeneous tumours and tracked the MYCN-amplified clone's dynamics in each, revealed the conditions that favour its growth, and tested its responses to 5000 drug combinations.
